# Everything That Happened in AI Today (Thursday, November 12, 2026)

United restricted unauthorized AI agents from booking flights; Databricks introduced an always-on business assistant; Google unveiled AlphaGenome 2; and a Federal Reserve official warned about AI investment risks.

...

## Around the Horn: Thursday, November 12, 2026

United Airlines is refusing to let unauthorized AI agents book flights, even as companies such as OpenAI and Meta develop assistants that can handle increasingly complicated tasks for users.

The airline says AI assistants can display its flight options, but customers must complete purchases themselves. United cited concerns about personal information, accidental bookings, and aviation regulations. Passengers also have to complete required declarations, including confirming that checked luggage contains no explosives.

United CEO Scott Kirby also said he doesn't want another middleman between the airline and its customers. Although United has reportedly seen relatively few attempts to book flights through personal AI agents, its decision could affect how these assistants develop.

And there's a question here beyond airline tickets. If your AI assistant already knows your travel preferences and payment information, how much authority should it have to complete purchases? United says it may reconsider its policy as the technology improves. For now, the airline wants a human at checkout.

### 🏆 TOP 5 NEWS (Around the Horn)

1. Nvidia's board is reportedly preparing to remove CEO Jensen Huang following allegations involving his personal relationships and an ongoing security investigation. His potential departure could leave the AI chipmaker facing an unexpected leadership change.
2. A Federal Reserve official warned that AI investments could trigger a market correction if financial returns fail to meet expectations. Fed Governor Michelle Bowman raised concerns about AI-related debt and inflated valuations just as Anthropic prepares for one of the largest initial public offerings in history.
3. A proposed bill could require federal permission to train advanced AI models. Democratic lawmakers are considering legislation to create a Department of Artificial Intelligence with authority to regulate the development of advanced models. The draft includes substantial penalties for violations, but its political support and prospects for passage remain uncertain.
4. US corporate AI spending reached another record in October, but monthly growth slowed to just 1.65%, according to Ramp's AI Index. The top 1% of companies still account for 80% of OpenAI and Anthropic revenue in Ramp's data. Customer support is emerging as a faster-growing use case, though it generally relies on less expensive models than software development.
5. CoreWeave is asking AI customers to pay upfront and pursuing shorter contracts to finance its computing infrastructure. The company expects roughly $9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits over the next three months. Its quarterly revenue rose 168% year over year to $3.66 billion, but it also reported a $709 million net loss.

...

- Databricks introduced an always-on version of Genie. The AI agent can work in the background, retrieve company information, and pursue longer assignments. Its new Ontology capability helps it understand relationships between employees, projects, and organizational data. In a TechCrunch demonstration, CEO Ali Ghodsi used Genie to examine disappointing employee survey responses and investigate a lost sales opportunity. Existing Genie capabilities are generally available, while the new always-on experience is headed for preview and beta programs.
- Google introduced the Gemini Decisions API for applications that need quick decisions rather than lengthy generated answers. Developers can evaluate up to 1,000 yes/no questions, multiple-choice decisions, or scoring criteria in one request. The API accepts text and multimedia inputs, returns confidence scores, and starts at $0.10 per million input tokens.
- Google DeepMind unveiled AlphaGenome 2, a DNA analysis model that predicts how genetic variations affect individual cell types. Google says it identifies nearly twice as many variants that influence gene expression compared with its previous model. Scientists can access it for noncommercial research, but the model has not been approved for clinical diagnosis.

## Developer & DevOps News Top 5

- AWS Open-Sources an Official AWS Emulator — Every Line Written by Autonomous Agents (Nov 11)

About Amazon GitHub HN, 764 points

AWS Emulator is a first-party local emulator of AWS APIs: point the AWS CLI or any SDK at its endpoint via environment variables and run your code against in-memory emulated resources — no AWS account, no network calls, no service fees. It’s Rust, CC0-1.0 licensed, 2,674 stars since going public, with RPM/Debian packages, a Docker image for macOS/Windows, an embedded mode for Rust SDK tests, published per-release fidelity scores, and an install-and-connect skill for AI coding agents. The build story is the second headline: Amazon says thousands of autonomous agents on Bedrock AgentCore wrote every line of it, and agents keep it updated many times a day as AWS services change. Limits are stated plainly — it doesn’t evaluate IAM policies (don’t test security against it), it’s single-region/single-account, and everything vanishes when it stops.

...

- Node.js Ships 16 Fixes Across 22.x, 24.x, and 26.x — HTTP/2 Bugs Can Leak TLS Keys and Response Memory (Nov 11)

Node.js blog pre-alert

The updates are available now: 7 high, 6 medium, and 3 low, with HTTP/2 taking the worst of it. A re-entrancy flaw in HTTPS lets an unauthenticated client make a server copy its own heap — including TLS private keys and other connections’ requests — into a response body (CVE-2026-123864); HTTP/2 stream teardown can send freed response buffers from other connections to a peer (123866); `respondWithFile()` servers get a remote use-after-free (123874); and TLS 1.2

title: AI News Today (Nov 12, 2026): OpenAI $10B, TSMC AI Bet – Kill The AI
text:
AI news today, November 12, 2026: OpenAI's quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion, TSMC approved up to $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI investments, and Google released AlphaGenome 2. Here are the 10 top stories and 5 security stories, each with free, non-paywalled sources.

## Key Takeaways

- OpenAI's quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion for the first time, up almost 50% from Q2.
- TSMC's board approved up to $1 billion in investments in Anthropic and OpenAI.
- Google's AlphaGenome 2 predicts how DNA variants affect specific cell types.
- England's universities regulator urged a return to traditional exams and in-person presentations.
- Railway said stolen AI keys led to about $740,000 in unauthorized charges.

## 1. OpenAI Quarterly Revenue Tops $10 Billion

OpenAI's quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion for the first time, up almost 50% from $6.7 billion in the second quarter, according to reports. Enterprise sales drove the increase, and ChatGPT now has 100 million paying subscribers, The Decoder reports.

The growth came with a $10.9 billion adjusted operating loss, and OpenAI still trails Anthropic, which reported $17 billion in revenue over the same period. OpenAI is cutting prices and adding enterprise products as it prepares for an IPO next year.

...

## 2. TSMC Bets Up to $1 Billion on Anthropic and OpenAI

TSMC's board approved up to $1 billion in AI investments: $500 million for Anthropic common shares at its IPO price and $500 million for OpenAI preferred stock. The chipmaker said both investments remain subject to the terms of the offerings.

...

## 3. AlphaGenome 2 Predicts DNA Effects by Cell Type

Google DeepMind released AlphaGenome 2, a model that predicts how DNA variants affect specific human cell types and states. It was trained on more than 100 million cell profiles across 68 tissues and identifies nearly twice as many expression-changing variants as its predecessor.

The model is available for non-commercial research through the AlphaGenome API, with a private preview for commercial use.

...

## 4.

...

England's Office for Students told universities to return to traditional exams and in-person presentations after an investigation found AI made coursework "close to impossible" to assess. A survey of more than 300 respondents at 127 institutions found students used AI heavily and often undetected.
